title: A randomised clinical trial to evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of the use of synthetic tape during anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstructive surgery
official: Synthetic Tape Reconstruction Augmentation in Primary ACL injuries: a randomised trial
summary:
Background and study aims
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is a strong band of tissue inside the knee that helps keep it stable. Sometimes, the ACL can tear and needs an operation, called ACL reconstruction (ACLR). In this operation, the torn tissue is replaced. Some people, however, still feel that their knee is weak or wobbly after the operation, or they find it hard to get back to their usual activities.

One way which may help this issue is adding a strong, man-made tape to help the new tissue heal. The idea is that this tape stops the new tissue from stretching too much and helps protect it. This tape is being used more often by surgeons to treat ACL tears.
 
However, we are not yet sure whether the tape helps, and that is why we are doing this study. We want to look at whether the tape helps patients’ knees heal better, and if there are any limitations to this, for example their activity levels. We also want to look at whether the tape is worth the extra cost to the NHS

Who can participate?
We are recruiting patients who have an ACL tear and are scheduled for an ACLR operation into the STRAP ACL study. Patients will receive their ACLR operation with or without the tape.

What does the study involve?
To help us measure whether the tape is clinically and cost-effective, we will ask participants to complete questionnaires before and 3, 6, 12 and 18 months after their operation. At 18-months after their operation they will need to attend a clinic for something called a pivot shift test, which is a routine test carried out in people with ACL tears, and it helps to assess how stable the knee is.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Both types of operations (with tape and without tape) are normally done in NHS hospitals. Joining the study doesn’t make participants’ treatment riskier, because they are getting the standard care for their ACL. There are no direct benefits from taking part, however what we learn could help future patients with knee injuries and participants will be reimbursed for their time in the form of vouchers.

Where is the study run from?
University of Warwick (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2026 to October 2029

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research (UK)

Who is the main contact?
strapacl@warwick.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. People (aged >=16 years) with an ACL rupture (diagnosed clinically, with MRI confirmation of injury to ACL) requiring ACLR
2. Provision of written informed consent
3. Able to access and willing to complete electronic questionnaires
4. Understands written English, or with support from family or friends
Exclusion criteria:
1. Revision ACL reconstruction
2. Multi-ligament injury requiring surgery to another major knee ligament such as concomitant posterior cruciate or collateral ligament surgery
3. Knee injury requiring cartilage repair surgery, except simple debridement, or concurrent patellar instability surgery
4. Previous surgery on the same knee except minor arthroscopic procedures (in the opinion of the treating clinician): limited to arthroscopy alone, removal of loose bodies and/or partial meniscectomy 
5. Unable to adhere to trial protocols or completion of questionnaires (the need to offer translations will be kept under review by the trial team) 
6. Previous randomisation in the present trial (i.e. other knee)
